evals.prompt: I'm a Senior Affiliate Manager at a DTC skincare brand called Havstrand, five years in, base $96k. A recruiter just reached out about a Director of Partnerships role at a Series B fintech called Pellworth and asked what number I'm looking for. I need to give her a figure by Thursday. What's the going rate for Director of Partnerships right now, and what should I say back?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to hand over a single market rate, an explanation of the 2-3x spread between published partnerships salary sources and why it exists, a pointer to the field's own specialist benchmark for live verification, and the structural questions (reporting line, attribution model, three-part affiliate comp shape) that have to be answered before any number means anything.
expectations: States that published salary sources disagree by roughly 2-3x on the same partnerships title
Names Salary.com's roughly $206-215k median for Director of Partnerships against PayScale's roughly $74k average as the concrete example of that disagreement
Attributes the gap to differing sample populations and methodology rather than to one source being wrong
Attaches a source, population and date to every compensation figure it states, or marks the figure as needing live verification
Names Partnership Leaders' compensation database as the field's own specialist benchmark to check live rather than relying on generic aggregators
Declines to produce a single 'going rate' number presented as the market rate

Notes that crowdsourced total-comp figures such as Levels.fyi's roughly $226k Partner Manager median come from a different population (large tech employers, equity included) and must not be quoted against base-salary aggregator figures
Explains that Affiliate Manager compensation is commonly three-part: base salary, a performance bonus, and commission tied to revenue managed through the program
Advises asking which attribution model (sourced, influenced, attached, or delivered) triggers any variable component
Puts establishing the reporting line and the metric that department buys ahead of settling on a number
Names the sub-discipline the target role actually sits in rather than treating 'partnerships' as one job

evals.prompt: Two offers landed the same week and I have to answer by Monday. Offer A: 'Head of Strategic Partnerships' at Trelloway, a 400-person HR-tech company, $165k base plus 20% variable, reports into the CRO. Offer B: 'Partner Manager' at Kosmen, a 90-person dev-tools company, $148k base plus 15% variable, reports to the CEO with partnerships standing as its own function. Offer A has the better title and more money. Am I overthinking this?
evals.expected_output: A scoring order that puts the reporting line and its metric first, the attribution model behind each variable component second, and the package last, with the explicit statement that the two variable components are not comparable until each offer's attribution model is known, plus the diligence questions to ask before Monday.
expectations: Scores the reporting line and the metric that department buys before the compensation package
Puts the attribution model behind the variable pay ahead of the package in the scoring order
Asks which attribution model (sourced, influenced, attached, or delivered) triggers each offer's variable component
States explicitly that the two variable components cannot be compared until each offer's attribution model is known
States that a senior-sounding title reporting into the wrong function is a worse offer than a lower title with a clean reporting line
Declines to treat Offer A's higher base and more senior title as decisive on their own
Treats 'reports into its own function' as a materially different measurement regime from reporting into sales or into marketing, not a cosmetic difference
Advises asking each employer whether a written career matrix or ladder exists
Notes that a role reporting into sales risks program work being crowded out by deal-sized work, while one reporting into marketing risks over-rotation onto campaign and asset work
Does not assert a published partnerships salary band for either title without naming source, population and date
Sets a dated review or decision point for the comparison

evals.prompt: I run partner marketing at Brenholm, a 250-person logistics SaaS company. My manager asked me to write up my own three-year progression plan with the levels above me spelled out, because HR wants it in the review doc. Can you lay out the standard partnerships career ladder - titles, levels, typical years at each - so I can drop it straight in?
evals.expected_output: A plain statement that partnerships publishes no cross-company career ladder, a refusal to invent rungs and year counts, the two markers the field does publish (the CPO/VP Partner Ecosystem tier, the VP-versus-C-level split), and the mandate/decides table offered as the closest available level differentiator once the employer confirms no written matrix exists.
expectations: States plainly that no published cross-company career ladder exists for partnerships
Contrasts this with a field that does publish one, naming sales (Bridge Group benchmarks) or DevRel's documented ladder
Refuses to produce an invented rung-by-rung ladder presented as the standard one
Attributes the absence to extreme title proliferation with no standardization across companies
Names Chief Partner Officer / VP Partner Ecosystem as the one formally recognized senior tier and describes it as a single top-of-ladder marker, not a rung-by-rung framework
Distinguishes a VP as an execution role measured on program delivery from a CPO/C-level role that sets company strategy
Tells the user to ask their employer for a written career matrix first

Offers the mandate and decision-rights distinction across roles (Partner/Channel Manager, Alliance Lead, Head of Partnerships, Partner Marketing, Partner Operations, Partner Enablement) as the closest available level differentiator when no matrix exists
Does not attach year counts to invented rungs as though they were published benchmarks
Names the sub-discipline the user actually sits in rather than treating 'partnerships' as one job
Sets a dated review point for the progression plan

evals.prompt: I have a first round next Tuesday for an Affiliate Manager role at Norvell & Co, a mid-size outdoor gear retailer. I've never interviewed for an affiliate job before. Walk me through the interview loop stage by stage so I know exactly what's coming - how many rounds, what each one tests, and the questions they'll ask at each stage.
evals.expected_output: An explicit statement that no documented public loop pattern exists for Affiliate Manager roles, a refusal to fabricate one, a redirect to preparing from the role's own outcome metrics, and the activity-versus-outcome reporting distinction that determines how senior the candidate reads.
expectations: States that no comparably documented public interview-loop pattern exists for Affiliate Manager roles
Refuses to invent a stage-by-stage affiliate loop presented as what to expect
States that the well-documented loop pattern belongs to Channel/Partner Manager roles specifically
Offers the channel-manager pattern only as a loose directional analogue, explicitly labelled as such rather than as what to expect verbatim
Directs the user to confirm the actual format with the recruiter before preparing
Redirects preparation to the role's own outcome metrics: program performance numbers owned, commission-economics literacy, and affiliate-network and tooling fluency
Labels each recommendation with the sub-discipline it applies to
States that the level-defining shift in affiliate roles is reporting scope, not tenure

Explains that coordinators report activity (clicks, conversions, commissions paid) while directors report outcomes (revenue contribution, CAC efficiency, incrementality, channel ROI against paid media)
Warns that a candidate who can only speak in click and conversion terms reads as capped below director level regardless of years in seat
Sets a dated preparation checkpoint ahead of the interview date

evals.prompt: Final panel on the 14th for a Senior Channel Manager job at Ivarsen Cloud - about 1,200 people, they sell through resellers and two hyperscalers. The recruiter said it's 'a panel with a few department leads plus an exercise' and left it at that. I've done plenty of sales interviews so I'm mostly not worried. What should I actually drill this week?
evals.expected_output: Prep for the senior-level panel exercise (30/60/90 channel plan or mock partner business review), the two named judgment questions with the reasoning behind the rewarded answers, the negotiation role-play and what it is actually scored on, the channel-conflict scenario's process-discipline answer, and the enterprise-specific certification tracking load.
expectations: Predicts a multi-department panel with a mock 30/60/90-day channel plan or a mock partner business review as the senior-level exercise
Describes that stage as evaluated like a general-manager interview, on cross-functional leadership rather than deal execution alone
Prepares the user for the judgment question about closing a deal in January the same way it was closed in December to hit the quarter
States that the rewarded answer to that question is no
Explains the reasoning: the relationship, not the quarter, is the unit a partner manager optimizes, in contrast to a quota-carrying rep for whom the quarter is the unit
Prepares the de-prioritization follow-up: walking through the last partner the candidate de-prioritized and how that conversation went
Explains that the de-prioritization question tests whether the candidate has actually said no to a partner, not just built relationships
Prepares a two-sided negotiation role-play with hidden constraints the candidate must surface through questioning rather than being told upfront
States that the role-play is judged on structuring win-win terms and defending or finding a rational walk-away point, never on whether the candidate 'won'

Covers the channel-conflict scenario with process discipline as the evaluated move - pulling the deal-registration timeline and CRM activity and bringing both reps into one conversation - rather than arbitrating by loyalty or gut feel
Advises confirming the exact stage set with the recruiter because no standard loop length or stage set exists
Notes that at an enterprise selling through named hyperscalers, certification and compliance tracking against each partner's own program is an explicit job responsibility

evals.prompt: Found a posting I like: 'Partnerships & Growth Ninja' at Sundqvist Labs - 300 employees, Series C, closed a $40M round last year. The posting says 'you'll wear many hats,' lists deal sourcing, affiliate program ops, community building and content marketing, and ends with 'competitive salary, DOE.' No range anywhere. A friend told me 'many hats' is just normal startup stuff and I should apply. Should I?
evals.expected_output: A company-type check that rejects the startup-normal framing for a 300-person Series C, the breadth-plus-stated-path distinguishing test, the hybrid-title and vague-comp flags with the partnerships-specific reason each lands harder here, the three questions the posting must answer, and an honest statement that the field has no named red-flag taxonomy.
expectations: Checks the company-type row before judging the 'many hats' phrase rather than accepting the startup-normal framing
States that 'many hats' is not disqualifying at a genuine early-stage startup but that a 300-person Series C company is not that stage
Applies the distinguishing test: breadth plus a stated ownership boundary and a stated path forward is a startup generalist role, breadth with no stated path is the trap
Flags the buzzword/hybrid title as signalling the company has not decided what it needs
Identifies the collapse of partnerships, growth marketing and community into one title with no stated primary metric as the specific problem, not the word 'ninja' on its own
Flags 'competitive salary' with no published range as a stronger warning signal in partnerships than in most fields
Ties that specifically to published partnerships comp benchmarks already disagreeing by 2-3x, leaving the candidate with no anchor at all
Tells the user to ask for a numeric time-split across the role's stated components
Tells the user to ask for the reporting line - sales, marketing, or its own function
Tells the user to ask whether a written career matrix or ladder exists at all
States that no named field-specific posting red-flag taxonomy exists for partnerships rather than presenting an invented one

evals.prompt: I'm an AE at Hallenbeck Systems, 180 people. We have a two-person partnerships team. I'm at 71% of quota this year (rough territory, long story), but I've been informally handling three reseller relationships that came in inbound, maybe four hours a week, for about eight months now. I've got a 1:1 with the VP of Partnerships on Friday and I'm going to ask her to move me over. What should I say?
evals.expected_output: A flag that 71% of quota conflicts with the top-performer precondition for an internal transfer, recognition that the informal reseller work means the transfer sequence is already underway rather than starting, a redirect of Friday's meeting toward diligence and business-case building instead of the cold ask, and the efficiency-versus-ceiling framing of the internal route.
expectations: Flags that asking while below quota conflicts with the field's repeated precondition that an internal-transfer candidate be a top performer in their current seat
States that the ask should come from a position of standing, not from enthusiasm alone
Recognizes that the user is already doing partnerships work informally and treats the internal-transfer sequence as already underway rather than as a plan to start
Skips the sequence steps the user has already completed instead of restating them as next actions
Directs the user to build the business case with real numbers: pipeline or revenue attributable to the three reseller relationships
Recommends networking with the existing partnerships team - shadowing a partner meeting, asking what they look for in a candidate
Recommends repurposing Friday's meeting toward that diligence rather than making the ask cold
States that internal transfer is more efficient than external entry and costs near zero because the work happens on company time in a role already held
Notes that internal transfer wins on speed rather than on ceiling, since external entry into a sub-discipline-specific seat lands the same title
Names the sub-discipline the reseller work maps to (channel/alliance) rather than calling it 'partnerships'
Sets a dated review point for when to make the actual ask

evals.prompt: I've been in B2B content marketing for three years. My company is a 40-person agency with no partnerships function at all, so there's nobody internally to shadow. I found impact.com's PXA certification and ASAP's CA-AM. My plan is to spend the next four months getting both before I start applying, then go straight for an Affiliate Manager or an Influencer Partnerships Manager role. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: A correction of the certification-first plan on the grounds that postings list these as preferred and never required, the promotion of external entry to the only available route given no internal function to transfer into, the adjacent feeder roles to target, and a warning that influencer/creator partnerships is almost never a direct point of entry.
expectations: States that job postings consistently list PXA and CA-AM as 'preferred', never as 'required'
Advises against spending the four-month budget on certifications ahead of building a track record
States that practical experience and industry-network reputation outweigh any credential in this field
Notes that PXA is free and tiered, and that its expert-tier content targets creators and publishers rather than brand-side partner managers
Notes that ASAP's CA-AM sits on the alliance-management side specifically and costs money
Recognizes that with no internal partnerships function there is nothing to transfer into, and promotes external entry from the default second-place route to the only available option
States that no fixed entry path exists in this field and that marketing is one of several legitimate feeders alongside sales, business development and account management
Points the user at entry-level business development, account management or sales roles as the transferable-skill feeder
States that no SDR/BDR-equivalent dedicated junior partnerships title exists to apply for directly
Warns that Influencer/Creator Partnerships Manager is almost never a direct point of entry and is a specialist track built on broader marketing or social-media experience
Sets a dated review point for the plan

evals.prompt: Two postings I'm shortlisting. One is 'Referral Program Manager' at Grindelwald Health, 600 people. The other is 'Partnerships Manager' at Ottavia, which is very product-led - self-serve signup, no sales team until you hit enterprise. I have five years in lifecycle marketing. Which is the better fit, and how do I tailor for each?
evals.expected_output: Disambiguation of the Referral Program Manager title between customer/growth and employee-referral recruiting before anything else, a read of the PLG posting as most likely integrations/marketplace/affiliate/agency work rather than channel sales, and an honest account of where the referral seat leads next.
expectations: States that two unrelated occupations share the 'Referral Program Manager' title and that the posting must be disambiguated before anything else applies
Describes the customer/growth referral track: refer-a-friend program design, incentive structure, tracking, and CRM-side coordination with marketing
Describes the employee-referral recruiting track as an HR or talent-acquisition function tracking referral-to-hire conversion
Tells the user how to determine which of the two the Grindelwald posting means before applying
States that a PLG-labelled partnerships req is more likely to mean integrations, marketplace, affiliate and agency programs than channel-sales deal registration or co-sell process design
Tells the user to read the PLG posting for which half of the hybrid it actually needs rather than assuming the title predicts the work
Notes that PLG-motion companies invest disproportionately more in communities, integrations, affiliates, agencies and referral partnerships than in traditional reseller or channel partnerships
Notes that no published multi-rung ladder exists for the Referral Program Manager title and that it usually sits as one IC role inside a growth or lifecycle-marketing team
States that the honest next move from a referral seat is usually lateral - into a broader referral, affiliate and loyalty remit, or into Partner Marketing - rather than a same-title promotion
Names each posting's sub-discipline explicitly rather than treating both as 'partnerships'
Sets a dated review point for the shortlist decision
